analysis.one_liner: Requires electronics makers to sell parts, tools, and repair manuals to owners and independent shops.
analysis.headline: The bill has just 2 cosponsors and has sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee with no hearing or vote since its February 2026 referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Repair Act would require makers of digital electronics — phones, laptops, appliances, and anything else that runs on digital electronics — to sell spare parts, repair tools, and service manuals to device owners and independent repair shops on the same terms they give their own authorized repair networks. It would also ban software tricks like "parts pairing," where a manufacturer programs a device to reject or downgrade a working replacement part that didn't come from the factory. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general would enforce the rules. The bill excludes motor vehicles, medical devices, and several other categories, and shields manufacturers from liability for damage caused by independent repairs.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of phones, laptops, tablets, appliances, and other digital electronics gain the right to fix their own devices or take them to any local shop, with access to the same parts, tools, and manuals the manufacturer gives its authorized dealers. Independent repair businesses gain access to parts and documentation at terms no worse than authorized dealers get, which lets them compete on price and turnaround time. The bill defines "fair and reasonable terms" as the best price and conditions the manufacturer offers anyone, so independent shops could not be priced out. Consumers who currently face the choice of an expensive manufacturer repair or buying a new device would see more repair options and more competition.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Device owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers must make documentation, parts, and tools — including updates — available to owners and independent repair providers on terms equivalent to the best terms they give their own authorized repair network [S2].

The bill bans parts pairing and similar software locks that keep a working replacement part from functioning, degrade device performance after an independent repair, or trigger false warnings and extra repair fees [S2].

The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the requirements as unfair or deceptive practices, and every state attorney general could sue violators in federal or state court to stop them, win civil penalties, and recover money for state residents [S2].
Manufacturers cannot escape the rules through contracts — any arrangement with authorized repair providers that tries to waive the manufacturer's obligations under the act is void [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Electronics manufacturers — makers of phones, computers, appliances, and other digital devices — would have to sell parts, tools, and manuals at prices and terms at least as favorable as those given to their authorized dealers, ending practices like parts pairing that steer repairs into their own channels. They would lose some repair revenue and some of the advantage that pushes customers toward buying new devices instead of fixing old ones, and would bear the cost of publishing documentation and distributing parts more widely. Consumers doing their own repairs or using independent shops would bear the risk when a repair goes wrong, because the bill blocks manufacturers from being liable for damage or data breaches caused by independent repair work.

drawbacks.text: The bill shields manufacturers from liability for damage, injury, data loss, or data breaches that result from work done by independent repair providers or owners, and requires no warranty on independent repairs — so if a third-party repair goes badly, the device owner generally has little recourse against the maker [S2].

Large categories are carved out entirely: motor vehicles, medical devices, off-road and non-road vehicles such as motorcycles, boats, aircraft, and ATVs, and emergency communications equipment are all excluded, so owners of those products get no new repair rights [S2].

The manufacturer's duty to open up security locks applies only 'as necessary' and the bill preserves trade secrets, which leaves room for manufacturers to argue that security-sensitive tools and documentation cannot be shared with independent shops — a real constraint on how much repair access this actually creates [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and broad: almost every device an ordinary household owns would become cheaper and easier to fix, and small repair shops would get a fair shot at the parts and manuals they need. The bill is not badly designed — it has genuine enforcement power through the FTC and state attorneys general, and it closes the contract loophole manufacturers otherwise use. But the liability shield is a serious concession: owners who choose independent repair take on the risk themselves, and the exclusions for cars, medical devices, and farm-adjacent equipment leave out some of the products where repair costs bite hardest. On balance it would help working people, with costs concentrated on manufacturers, though the help is narrower than the bill's title suggests.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in February 2026 and has stayed there with no hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Joseph Morelle of New York introduced the Fair Repair Act on February 5, 2026, joined by Representative Perez; it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1].
The bill has exactly 2 cosponsors, both Democrats, and no further action has been taken since the referral — no committee hearing, markup, or vote appears in the action history [S3].
Congress runs through January 3, 2027, so the bill is still technically alive, but it currently has no committee activity and no path to the floor [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Electronics manufacturers are ahead so far: with the bill parked in committee, no repair-access or anti-parts-pairing rules have taken effect, and manufacturers continue to control who can buy parts and perform repairs. Device owners continue to face the current repair options and prices.

for.name: Rep. Joseph Morelle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Repair Act on February 5, 2026

for.name: Rep. Perez
for.what_they_did: Joined as a cosponsor at introduction

against.name: Digital electronics manufacturers and industry groups
against.role: Device makers such as phone and computer manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Industry groups representing device makers have opposed federal right-to-repair bills like this one in past Congresses, arguing that third-party repair threatens safety and data security

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the bill's only 2 cosponsors are Democrats, but no votes have been held, so the partisan shape of support and opposition is not yet known.

analysis.trajectory: Almost certainly stays in committee. Bills referred to Energy and Commerce with only a handful of cosponsors and no scheduled hearing rarely reach the floor, and previous versions of the Fair Repair Act in earlier Congresses never got a vote. Unless committee leadership schedules action or the bill attracts many more cosponsors this session, it will die when the 119th Congress ends on January 3, 2027, and would need to be reintroduced.
